reading.rtitle: The Order You Read It In
paras: Every contract you will ever read is built out of four things, and only one of them is written to be interesting. There is what each side promises to do. There is what happens if somebody does not do it. There is the machinery — notice, governing law, assignment, all the paragraphs that are skipped on a first reading. And there is the part that decides how much anybody can lose. Lawyers who are new to the work read a contract from the first line to the last, in order, at the same speed. Lawyers who have been doing it for ten years do not read it in that order at all.

The words that carry the weight are almost all modal verbs, and they are not interchangeable. Shall and must create an obligation: somebody has to do this. May creates a permission: somebody is allowed to, and nobody is forcing them. Is entitled to is a right that belongs to one party whether the other side likes it or not. Shall not is a prohibition. Change one of those words and you have changed what the company is committed to, which is why a translated contract is dangerous long before anybody notices: Portuguese solves obligation and permission with the same handful of verbs, and English does not.

The most expensive paragraph is usually the shortest. A cap on liability is one sentence, and it decides the size of the worst day of the relationship. An indemnity is one sentence, and it moves somebody else's loss onto your balance sheet. A remedy clause is one sentence, and it can quietly say that the only thing you are entitled to is your money back, no matter what the breach cost you. None of those sentences look important. They look like boilerplate, which is exactly the problem: boilerplate is what nobody reads, and it is where the risk is parked.

So the order matters. Read the termination clause first, because it tells you how you get out and what it costs. Then the liability cap and the indemnity, because together they tell you the worst case. Then the governing law, because it decides who is going to be reading this clause if the two of you ever disagree about it. Only after that is it worth reading the promises at the front, which is the part everybody starts with and the part that changes least.

listenings.text: If you gave me a hundred-page agreement and ten minutes, I would not read the first page. I would go straight to termination, then to the liability cap, then to the governing law, and I would already know more about the deal than somebody who had read forty pages in order. Termination tells me how this ends and what it costs to leave. The cap tells me the size of the worst possible day. The governing law tells me whose rules we are arguing under if it goes wrong. Everything at the front is what the two sides are enthusiastic about, and enthusiasm is the part that changes least in a negotiation. I am not saying skip it. I am saying it is not where the risk lives, and reading it first is how you run out of attention before you get to the paragraph that matters.

The worst mistake I have seen in a translated contract was one word long. The English said that either party may terminate on ninety days notice. The Portuguese version came back saying that either party had to terminate on ninety days notice. Nobody noticed for two years, because for two years nobody wanted to leave. When one side finally did, both companies were reading the same agreement and seeing different obligations, and the argument was not about the business at all. It was about a modal verb. That is why I never translate shall, may and must by feel. Obligation, permission and prohibition are three different commitments, and in English they are three different words. If the person drafting cannot tell you which of the three a clause is doing, the clause is not finished yet.

extra_audio.text: The agreement arrives and nobody has time to read a hundred pages. The termination clause is read first: how it ends, and what leaving costs. The liability cap and the indemnity are read next, because together they show the worst case. The governing law is checked, because it decides whose rules an argument happens under. And only then are the promises at the front of the contract worth reading.
